title: Dave Bailey and John McNeil Interview, 1959-10-25

pages.label: 001_Dave Bailey and John McNeil Interview, 1959-10-25 Part 1

blocks.x: Let me see, this is Dick Allen. We're doing an interview today. And what's your name?
Marjorie Zander.
All right. And what's your name? David Bailey. David Bailey, huh? And let's see, today is October the 25th, 1959. And our address, we're up there on South
Robertson, huh? 3418 South Robertson.
3418 South Robertson. I even knew what street we were on today. All right, so, uh, we usually start off by asking a guy his exact date of birth. The what? The exact date of birth.

Birth? Mm-hmm. Birth? You mean when he was born, you mean? Yeah, I mean. Well, I couldn't tell you that. You don't know? Because my mom and daddy died when I was a baby. And I never knew my mom and daddy. It was two old ladies. I knew my mom and daddy before I was born. And by me traveling, we were going to play music, you know, going out of town. But I still got my buss, I got upstairs there. By me traveling, playing music, going out of town. I rode to Washington, went down to the new city hall, new courthouse on Royal Street. Paid four dollars and rode all the way to Washington, come back and the city records went up, come back again. So I had to go to the new city hall back here. Mm-hmm. So they found my marriage, the ticket when I got married. Wow. So now, so now I got the right dope. So now I'm, I'm age 69 now.
Oh, you never knew that and you know you just have turned 69.
Oh yeah, just, just made it. They found my records when I got married. What was your birthday? Uh, it was on January the 28th.
January the 28th?
Yeah, 28th.
Mine's the 29th. Yeah. We're almost birthday pals.
I got my marriage thing up there. It's, it has the same as the birth certificate.
Well, we'll take a look at that if you, we'll take a look at that. When you, don't do it now, don't bother. Yeah. Okay, you want to get it? Yeah, right there. Now where were you born anyhow?
Right here in New Orleans.
Right here in New Orleans?
Uh huh. What neighborhood? Uh, it was Third and uh, Third and St. Thomas, my stepdad told me.
Third and St. Thomas?
Yeah, that's my stepdad told me. Mm-hmm.
Before he died.
I see. See, my mama was married twice. Oh yeah. After my mama and Bailey separated us, she, she married uh, Johnson. He did too.
And that's uh, must be Duck, Duck's Ernest's father, huh?
No, that's, my brother Ernest, see we're about the same mother, a different father. I see. See, uh, he's, he's a Johnson and I'm a Bailey.
Mm-hmm.

In other words, they claim when you're about the same mother, your whole brother's about the mother's side. We're about the same mother, a different father. I see. You're about the same mother, your whole, you're about the same father, a different way you have. I haven't seen him since 1927.
Where is he now?

He was in, he was in Ball, Oklahoma. And uh, he came back here once in 1927 to see me and he wanted to get me to go up there to play in a band with him. Mm-hmm. And I didn't want to leave. I was still working right at that hospital. I'm working now. He wanted to build up a home for me at all. I didn't want to leave. I suppose he must have gotten married and that's why he wasn't writing. Unless he might have lost the letters, you know, my address. Yeah. And I got it from my niece, his daughter. She was operating on the hospital that way. I got it from one, but by moving him up the town there, down here, I lost her. I can't find it. I had it in the book. Now, the only way I can get his address again, I have to try to get in touch with my niece, try to locate her. And get it again, you know, try to write it. Yeah.
We'd like to see him.
That's been a long time. How many years that's been? How long?
This is 59. That's somewhere around 32 years. Yeah. That's right. What year were you born in that? Let's get that straight. January.
What year though?
I got it on the thing.
You got it on the thing. Yeah, that's why I said Matt Neal must be gone.
Yeah.
He must have it.
Well, he'll be back then. Let's see. It's the birth certificate, you know. Now, do you remember this? I got married in 1910. I got married in 1910.
Yeah.
I got married in 1910.
I got married in 1910. I got married in 1910.
I got married in 1910. I got married in 1910.
I got married in 1910.
I got married in 1910. I got married in 1910. I got married in 1910.
I got married in 1910. I got married in 1910. Remember the Spanish American War?
No, nothing about that. No. You don't know? There were two wars I know that had. World War I and this war that had. World War II. I was talking Spanish American War. Well, I know a lot of the-
I had a grandpa.

My grandpa was in the D.A.s. He had big old, I forget what they call him, big old brother. They all tell him maybe, huh? I forget what they call them things. They shoot the trigger on the outside there. I forgot what they call them.
Cannons you mean? No.
They had one living on a camp place there. My aunt had it. Oh, I-
Musket.
I believe they called them muskets. Muskets in those days, huh?
Yeah.
It was in Spanish American War. Now let's see. There's one war I don't run by.
I thought maybe you remember that from a kid. No. From your days as a kid you might remember.

Uh-uh. I heard people talking about it when I was growing up. In the name of the two wars I know that was World War I and World War II. And I was scheduled to go in World War I. The week peace declared I was the leader next week.
How old were you when you were married? Twenty-one.
Yeah, twenty-one.
Mm-hmm. Now, uh-
I got examined at a big white school right down there on Dr. King Clio and the theater. Oh yeah, I know that school. That's where I got examined at. Mm-hmm.
Now, when you were young, what was the first music or singing that you remember hearing?
First music or singing?
Music or singing?
I'll tell you, I didn't pay much attention to anything like that. I was so busy getting up in the game myself.
You know?

And I used to play in the show. I used to play in church. I used to play in concerts, you know? Mm-hmm. Sing, dance, bunk dance. There's a great bunk dance. I used to be a great bunk dancer. Sing. And there's Lincoln Show and I used to be back on Lutheran Island and Howard. Mm-hmm. I used to play there every Friday night with the seven piece orchestra. That's when they had the Charleston out. That's a father named Foster Lewis and Dude Lewis.
I knew Dude, man. He used to play with Joe Avery and Wilbur Tillman. That's a guy I knew, Dude. Yeah, he's dead. I have a record in my collection of him.
Yeah, and his brother called him Foster Stan. He's dead too. The tribal place. They both buried.
I never knew Foster.
They both buried? Forst Stan.
Where are they buried?
Greenwood Cemetery. Both of them buried there.
Up there on?
Up in Corbin, up there, around the ice.
Green Street, huh?
Yeah, Greenwood Cemetery.
That's where?
That's where my stepdad is buried. And I got a son-in-law buried up there too.
Wesley Dimes is buried up there too, huh?
Wesley Dimes, he's dead?
Wesley Dimes was killed in Baton Rouge. You didn't know that years ago?
Yeah, I didn't know he was dead. Little Trump was playing him. Yeah. He's played on my brother.
Yeah, I saw his grave up there. Yeah, well you were- He was up there?
Yeah.
Yeah? How you got killed? He was killed by a policeman in Baton Rouge.
Yeah?
Shot him. That's what I heard.
Yeah, what's not coming?
Something to do with his wife, I think, or something. I don't know.
Yeah?
Well, you used to work with him in the Liberty Bell, somebody told me.
I don't know if that boy was dead. He'd been dead, eh? Yeah. A policeman shot him in Baton Rouge. Mm-hmm. That's what I heard.
He's been dead for quite a while. I wrote it all down from the grave, you know. All that.
He'd be a nice kid. I know he was a nice little trumpet player, Wesley Dimes. Yeah, I remember him.
I guess Eddie Morris told me about it, you know. He used to be with you, huh, in that band. Yeah.
He's pictures on there. You see his picture on there? When I showed you- did I show you the picture of the band? No. I never showed you the picture of the band.
You got a picture of the Liberty Bell?
No, I mean Eddie Morris when he was playing with us.
Oh yeah, that picture of the Gibson or the Jackson, I don't remember which it was. No, I never showed you the Liberty Bell.

I played with them. I played with them. I didn't play with them regularly, but the most I was playing with my brother, we had the Young Tuxedo. We was running this town. Wasn't none of them bands hardly could do anything with us. We had a good band. We used to play at Vicki Adams in the town of the Pawn Garden was open there, Aiden Rampo. We used to play there one time. Then we used to play for the Bulls. I played with Jack Carroll for quite a while and I played with Chris Kelly about six years. I played with Papa Celestine in the town of the district was open down there, a few close. He was running two bands. I played with him six months down there. And last year I was playing with Chris Kelly was on steam with Capitano in 1921.
Let's start back at the beginning. That might make it come out in better order, you know? So what was your very first instrument you played? Drums.
Drums. That's the first thing I took off, but I played a lot of them used after that.
You played another instrument, huh?
Yeah, I played harmonica, juice hop, flute, pipe, piccolo, baseball, guitar, piano.
Can you still play harmonica much?
Play the pool.
You want to make some records? I think I can fix you up. I bring my boy around sometime.

Yeah, I can play. I don't know how I would make out with the new teeth. After I get you up some teeth, I can't make it take teeth out and play like that. But the harmonica I used to play is a marine band. Oh yeah?
Mm-hmm.
I get a marine band receiver.
Well get in practice and phone me up at Tulane. You had to get in.
Yeah, you had to write it down.
Okay, we'll write it down. Hold on a second. What kind of guitar? You played a big wedding just with a…

Harmonica guitar followed by name Eddie Bole. He got mad and he moved and went to Iowa. You know where the Lightinghamer's Bakery shop is on Melpameen? And the Simon Bolegoire? Lightinghamer's Bakery?
I can't place… Oh yeah, I know that's at Melpameen. Is that the one?
There's a big tour of the house, two-star house right in the back of that between Simon Bolegoire and Liberty.
Mm-hmm.

We played a wedding up there, a house-packing game. Harmonica and Gipcho. And I had a derby put over the harmonica. And that guy played with the knife. And he was talking about some music. And we made some money that night.
Put a derby over the harmonica?
Yeah.
I've never heard of that.

Eat a can, get a can, anything. You know, this duck, be flowing this. You ever seen a trumpet player put the duck on? Yeah, sure. And I make that harmonica talk. I can play with my nose. Play with my north. Learned all that when I was a kid.
Oh yeah.

And I can imitate the train on harmonica. I can imitate the train on my snap drum. And I can take the trap, you know, the whole set, and play the whole part of high society. I can't do it. I can't do it.
What drum?
On the trap drums. I'll just let you know that I'm playing it. And I'll start off, if you understand, play the whole thing. Just by myself.
Can you play the drums and the harmonica at the same time?
Sure. If I had the rack, I'd have to have the rack. Yeah, do you have a rack? No, I have no rack. I might have to get you one.
I'll make you one out of a clothes hanger or something.
Yeah. I believe you can buy those things. Yeah, you can buy them.
I had one one time. Yeah.
Yeah, sure. I could play a harmonica, play a harmonica, play a harmonica. I like music, you know. Yeah. To do good at something, you got to like it. I guess that's why I do that thing.
Well now, when you were getting started, did you just pick up drums by yourself at first, or did you have a teacher?
No teacher. Just pick it up.
That's at first. Now, about how old were you when you started on drums?
I didn't know. I didn't know then.
Well, were you wearing long pants when you started? Oh no, I was a kid in short pants.
I started out a little bit of something. I started out when I just come up.
About three feet high, so, huh? Something like that.

I learned on tubs, tin pans, and boxes. Oh yeah, I see. Many people would throw the water at night. I'd be on people's step at 12 o'clock at night with some clean sticks. I was working at Old Magazine Market, trying to have the Old Magazine Market. I liked to have lost my job. I was delivering meat.
Yeah.

I got up to fill up in the non-station. He was having to stick in between the collar leg, you know, hold it laid open. They'd pine that these down. I seen a troubled trash. I ended up in the trash in the street. After I lived up with me, he got there and the girl and I was in the truck. I had to run in. And I got back, he says, I bet you've been playing drums. I said, Dave, if I didn't like you, he was a good boy, I'd fire. I said, I'll let this fly. I was about an hour or something back, he's going back.
I kept on trying to learn.

So my brother said, well I'm going to buy a little cheap drum. Cheap set. Went down to the pawn shop and got me a little old cheap snap drum. I got a little old bass drum. I made up a little band and I went on to the store and everything.
When you were what?

You know when I started trying to take a lesson? 1921 I was playing Chris Kelly. I was learning good. I was reading the music. I was reading. And everybody in the band could read it. See the trammel player from over the river, he used to buy the music and he arranged it. A brother named Harrison Bowen, he's a wife of Southern Pacific. And that guy was a good musician. Everybody in the band read it. We had Willie Foster. Willie Foster's brother, he was playing, you know, he'd read. And they got there and they showed me my drum pop. He used to hustle right down here, by that cemetery right down on Hallene Street, somewhere down there. And I'd hit that. Made note for note. But they told me I wouldn't need the music no more. So I just stopped. But every once in a while I look at over, I got five pieces of drum music right home now and my dresser drum. And that last drum I played on the steamer cap room. The people all stopped dancing, they all come around me. Where's that drum? The white man and the boss man both said, Son, did you read music right now? I said, no son, I'm just taking the lesson now. He said, well, Bobby Bobby, he said, my drum ain't got nothing on it, but the Zillow for me. You know, the thing made like Terry played them little balls. I told him, I said, allow me to break. I said, I'll play that. He said, I've got to give it to you. He said, you're a drummer. I played places where they can get the people back off me. I said, give me a room to play. And I tell them if they don't get the police to get back, I won't play. I said, I don't like the fair that, the Louisiana fair and the Porn Fair and the Run. He said, wipe over. He said, play a number on the band, on the fair. Play a number on the other people. Crying on the next side of the evening. I actually played the dances and the long part. Couldn't play. I played in Port Arthur, Texas. We played with the Black Eagle band, my brother and I. With E. Van? Yeah, I played with E. Van. So I played, but first we went there with our band.
Well, which was the Black Eagle? I'm trying to get that straight. Is that E. Van Thomas' Black Eagle or was that your ...?

No, E. T. Thomas, they called him that. It was his band. But we went over there, you know. And so we went there, we stayed four months. I think we were headquartered and left here. Put up four months over there, so.

pages.label: 002_Dave Bailey and John McNeil Interview, 1959-10-25 Part 2

blocks.x: Wait a minute, Jimmy Jackson what?

He's dead man, you know that? No. Sure, we played at the funeral. How long? It's going on six years now I believe it ought to be. The last time I saw his daughter at the hospital I believe she said it was going on five, and we're going on six now. Who's Gibson? That's the band I play in.
Yeah but who is Gibson that they named the band?
He just named the band that he named, the name Alphonse Spears, just named the band Gibson, the Gibson band.
Yeah but there's no such person as Gibson huh? No. Just made that up huh? Yeah. That's a kick. The Gibson band.

See because before it was named after Jackson, it was the Jackson band. You know what I'm saying? Yeah. Jimmy had a name behind him. His name was Alphonse Spears. I guess you didn't want to say Spears band, the name of the Egyptian band.
Well what did Jackson play?
Huh?
Did Jackson play music?
No. He knew how to play Snap a little bit. No he didn't play. He used to get the job. He'd get the job and he'd come in on it you know.
Did he ever work with you years ago or anything? No.

On Snap? No. In other words he just like a boss. He'd get the job. He'd be in the parade soon and have his little stick. Tell the boys what to play and all of them. And you know just like a grand marshal like that. He used to get all the jobs, get the wood. But one time he made a mess up at the Gordon District. He had two bands I was playing with playing too. I believe my band was in the front and he was behind. And he went and got that band. Called himself trying to do me a dirty trick. Something happened. I don't know if I was going to go rehearsing. I told him I couldn't make the rehearsals every Thursday like that. I'd be tired of working. You know what I mean? Hardest, other drum player in the band. And I was playing with a fella called Doc. Don't you know Doc?
No, what does he play?
Trumpet. Ernest Paulin is his name. He's calling him Doc.
Oh yeah, well I know Ernest Paulin. He lived right back here.

Back on Seventh Street out of the cemetery between Franklin and Liberty. Ernest Paulin is his name. They called him Doc. I was playing his band. And when he got through the Gondis, they weren't Jimmy Jackson's band no more. He was four, he signed a job for ten men and he brought nine. Well he got that money, man.
See?

He wouldn't hire that band no more. Then after that he come back and he won't try to get me to play back in the band with him again. None of the drummers do nothing with me. I ain't bragging on myself, not in the brass band. Not if I see if they, it's all that long they don't try to buck in. If I see where they're going to buck in, then I'm going to cover them up.
Well when you were a kid, did you follow any drummers around or anything?

Never just follow no parades when I was a kid. Never follow no parades around. Just go and look at them. See on Conville Day, hardly go and see Conville parades. I don't like to be in the monster gang of people. Never do. Can't stand to be amongst the crowd. Right now, when I'm working now at the hospital, the crowd go up on the elevator, I let them go up and I catch the next elevator. I never liked it from a kid up, never liked to be in the crowd. I used to go to theaters. Sometimes they had the, when they had the regular theaters like Chris and all them theaters. What'd I do? All these 50 shows? If you beat you amongst the crowd, I'll come back home. Never liked to be in the crowd, that's the fact. I don't even ride a crowded bus. Busy crowd, I won't get on. I'd rather be late going to work and get on crowded. But I don't know if this, don't like it. Don't like to be in the crowd. So it's all right as long as I know they don't try to buck against me, you see. If they go to work and try to buck, then I'm a couple of them. I beat a part playing during this church, we played at this church over here twice. I played in the Jackson band then. You know Kid Howell? It was his band. And you know this brother called Brother Conberry, played climate. He was playing with them. Pajo, all that was a band. He had a short duffer you know. I didn't have this set of drums, the other drums, but that big 28. I'll give it to a friend of mine. I let him out of that room too small. And the band, see we was the last band. The band, the first band, they were supposed to stop playing. The last band come up with the crew. After we come up with our crew they just kept on playing, pull on the side and kept on playing. I told the boy, I said don't stop playing, let's keep on playing. And I cut loose on that drum there. It was too bad. And when he tried to make what I'd make and I'd make different beats, I got him all kind of it. And he said, I told you you can't play no drums with that man. You just can't beat him. You've been playing since he was a little kid. You can't do it with him. That's a gift. And they all come in shaking hands with me. And when I was little, he called me, the boy about 12 or 13 years old, went up there and told my laddie, he said, Miss Margaret, Mr. Dave tied that band all up in the knot. He said, the band hadn't stopped playing. The band was trying to buck in and say, Mr. Dave cut loose on that drum and tied the whole drum. Everybody laughed. And the man that played so much drum, the man took me around the corner. And I said, come on boys, go with me. I got to give you something to drink. He carried the drum, brought me to his house. He had beer, he had home, I know what all that that band had in his place. Yeah. You want some whiskey? I know. You're the best drummer I've ever seen in this city.
Made that fella shame, that dog farm.
And you know little Jimmy, little Jimmy used to play your record, little short farm?
Oh yeah, Black Benny's buddy. Used to bum with Black Benny.

Yeah, little Jimmy. So I had him up right up here at the Middle of Dawn Church up there on Middle of Dawn Street. They had two bands. You know Minor? Played bass horn? They called him Gooey. You know Minor? Minor Anderson, yeah, big guy.
Played bass horn.

They called him Gooey. He lived up in town somewhere. So Jimmy was playing with him, you know. And we was in the league up there. But at least I had to stop playing. So Jim was playing with him, you know. And we was in the league, I believe. But at least I had stopped playing. And I got to lose all the drums, they gave me the drum solo. The people around me like that. Little Jim wasn't stood up to call him. He said he got to give it to him, he said he's the best, there ain't nothing to do like that man. That Jim is shamed. Now you know there's two guys I like to get to have a buck against. I wish I was going to ever catch him. This fella play Urica, Sun Fuqua over the corner. They told a guy to play Urica band and George Williams, you know what I mean. I want to get the buck against him. That's why they been bragging. Now this fella's son, he told a fella that lives out there, where I actually live. Down St. James Street. Told him one time he was waiting for the yellow cab. This fella was waiting for the yellow cab. He wasn't calling Pat. He said, you know what that guy told me to play Urica band? He said, he can beat you playing, playing drums. I said, yeah. I said, well that's not a musician. I said, you couldn't call that a musician. I said, a real musician ain't going to talk like that. He's there for the public. I said, that's Egan. I don't know what I mean to beat somebody doing. I said, if he's an accountant musician, he wouldn't pass that accountant.
Isn't that right?

That's right. He was a man who's supposed to praise himself. He's got to lead that to the public. I told him, I said, well, maybe someday you might see me playing. I said, I played with St. Paul's Church. Because St. Paul's Church they told him I was first to make. They were behind an other band, wasn't my band. I came out for listening and went out to James and the fellow was standing at the corner. I told him, boy, I said, play me a good number. Play me a good hammer. We started playing that thing about the singer. I got loose on that drum there. I went down to the grocery that Monday. Ain't that, is you the man playing that drum so yesterday? Yeah. Ooh, that man sure can beat a drum, kids. This fellow come up. Boy, give me your hand, sir. I've got to give it to you. He said, you can put that man in your pocket. He's talking about he can beat you playing drums, there you got a chance. You can put them in your right pocket and transport them to the left pocket.
They can't do it.

I like music, see. When you like something, you're about to do good at it, see. I'm crazy about music. I don't know. Just like that. Now of course on Sunday I don't bother playing that drum on Sunday. I'm getting up at the churches. You know, like Reverend Washington, that white Baptist church back on the Charles and General Poetry. I get all the Poetry, I get all the churches. I'm pulling those jazz on Sunday. Unless I, you know, I'll be playing for it. So any night, like, like, next week, any night, like I come home, where am I now? A good number come home, radio. Just play with my hand. Just hand on the wood and play all them rock and roll. I can play, I can play, I'm used to playing real good bands. I can't play no funny bands. You've got to be a real good band. I've played in bands where every tough song is on bottom. But the band, they don't play right, but I can't play a good drum. When we go around, we go around Huntsville, and when that band starts off, if they start the wrong key, I stop them and say, oh, if they're wrong key, get right. Let's get right. If they start the wrong key, I stop them right there. I can't play with them just playing in bands. The bands I used to play with my brother and that was the time the art followers used to parade and the Longshoremen, White and the, you call it Longshoremen, we used to turn out at the parade. We used to play for that pretty every year. The bands we had then, so these bands that got nothing, couldn't set aside one of them
bands. As I said, I played in some first class bands.

And I went away from here, I could have played in the Butterstock Band from Nashville, Mississippi, he used to play on Steamer Capital. He wanted me. I wanted to build up a home over there. And then Turt Johnson, the band, I don't know if he's from Baton Rouge, he wanted to fire his drum and take me. I was playing Jack Carey, I was playing Jack Carey, and my brother was playing bass, plays Brown. Then another place called, let me see, I believe it was Port Island, went to play. And there was a band up there that's called the Stores Band. They wanted me to play with them. I didn't want to leave town, they wanted me to stay up there, I didn't want to stay. I'm born and raised in New Orleans, I don't know how to play with New Orleans. I could have been to New York, I could have been to Chicago, I didn't want to leave. I could have been just like Lewis, my younger days. Brother Damon was up there, I said no. I said I don't want to make this stuff. So I went up there, I was a bit of a hump as a cat. I could have went up there and Lewis played with us. When he first came out of Jones, my brother was the first one to grab him. He had a little old brass on, all bent. He couldn't play with four or five numbers. My brother got in and broke him in. I had a brother broke with me, we should play with every side of the night over the river. The brick building, on the broken corner, every side of the night. And then we got broke in and got him a new home, made up a band. Went down to the winter count on the winter guard down there, Joe Oliver. Joe Oliver took him, he gave me food out there, Joe Oliver was all the last time I was just going there. But nobody learned me how to play. It's just a gift of all.
But what is the difference between your brother's age and yours?
I couldn't tell you on that.
Is he much younger than you or older?
I couldn't say it. Because see I left my people, I lost my people. Howdy, how you doing?
Okay, how you feeling? Alright.
I'm sweet as candy myself, I don't know how you are.
I'll see you then.
Hehehe. Say Mac, do you know what will become a high column, you think it's in that letter you got my, uh, Naps or Stippling Naps or what?
It may be.
Huh?
It may be.
It may be in that thing you got. Yeah.
Pull up a chair and uh... Yeah I was uh, went to get some bread and the bread wasn't ready. While I was waiting I went and made a few stops.
I told you that you're an insurance collector.
Yeah.
Yeah. Now let's get your name down, your full name first.
Uh huh. First name is John H. Mike Mill. Uh huh.
I see. And where were you born?
I was born in Glaston, Mississippi.
What county is that in?
That's in Emmett County.
And uh, exactly the date uh, you were born on?
I was born August the 22nd, 1916.
1916, I see. So you're considerably younger than Bailey. Fair much so, yeah. Uh, and how did you happen to get interested in music? Did you hear any music around when you were a kid?

Well my father was a musician and uh, he played music through the years. As a matter of fact my family, you know, all were musically inclined and practically everybody in the family played some type of musical instrument. And actually when I grew up I sort of became a part of me.
Uh huh.

And so I started taking lessons, you know, to learn how to play the trumpet. Of course my family was string musicians. My daddy was a piano player and mostly any strings instrument he could master. It was pretty good.
Who did your father play with?
Oh he mostly played with outfits of his own around the country, towns around the neighboring towns. No big, you know, never did go into it in a big band way. Yeah.
What was his name?
His name was John, senior, John H. Senior. Uh huh.
And uh, do you remember any of the tunes he'd play back in the days when you were young?

Oh yeah, he used to play a lot of the old stuff, blues numbers and uh, he loved waltzes. He used to play a lot of waltzes on the piano when I was a kid. And uh, he had quite a few numbers he played on his own that he never did amount to anything. Uh, his own version of the blues. Uh huh. Uh huh. And one number in particular he used to play sort of based on himself, you know.
How did that run? Can you sing a little bit of it?

Well it was just a blues number that he used to sing because of uh, of his uh, of his complexion. He was rather dark and he used to sing the blues about he was black but sweet oh lord. And it was, it became a typical blues number in that section you know.
Oh yeah. Yeah. Well I've heard that.
Yeah. Well he used to sing that quite a bit. My mother used to tell me about how he was black.
Did you know your father?
And he took a lot of pride in it huh? Yeah, my father's still living. He's in Chicago now. He's quite ageable now. He's up in the 70s.
I'd like to get his address in case uh, see I have a partner who goes up to Chicago once and while he'd like to meet him.
Yeah well, uh, want me to give you his address now or sometime later date?

Yeah, if you can get it probably. We'd like to get it whenever it's convenient. Yeah, I'll give it to you. Bailey's got my phone number. Uh huh. If you, if we don't get it today we'll get it another time. Yeah. I'll see you at the parade generally too.
Uh huh.
But, let's see now, he uh, he would be about what age now you figure?
Um, 70, he should be about 73 or better, better than 73.
Did he live here in the city ever?

No, he made frequent visits to New Orleans and uh, he got a lot of his ideas from New New Orleans because you know, he used to come here and uh, he, he sort of was a, even back in those days he was sort of like a booking agent for bands out of this section from around Baton Rouge, Scotlandville and, and uh, he used to book these bands to come up to my home and play for weekend engagements and uh, and everything. So, uh, and he would make quick trips down here making contact to get bands out of here to come up that way, to play dances and things. Oh yeah.
What bands would he hire? Do you remember?

Well, he used to hire quite a few of these, and back in those days they mostly had these string bands. And uh, uh, he, one guy in particular I can remember, you know, as a kid that used to hire quite a bit, used to come and fellow with, uh, his name was Dick Taylor. He played the violin, he was real good. And uh, some of, I don't remember the names of the other guys, but in those days they used the mandolin quite a bit. And uh, as a lead instrument. And my daddy, he played the mandolin and the bass violin.
Where was Dick Taylor from? Was he from New Orleans?
He was from around this section, around Scotlandville I think mostly. Uh huh.
Oh yeah, I've been up there.
Yeah.
Uh huh. And uh, did you ever hear Toots Johnson's band?

Not that I can recall. He was from Baton Rouge. I thought maybe he'd hired him. Probably there's a possibility, yeah. But like I said, I was, you know, relatively small because I came to New Orleans, uh, when I was about five, six years old. And then my daddy moved to Chicago and I went to Chicago and live a while. And I came back to New Orleans when I was around eleven. And then I started to, uh, go into grade school. Here over at Tom Lafon, that's when I started my musical career. Well, we first Negro school that had organized a band in the school. Because today all the schools have bands. We were the first band, school band that was organized among Negroes in the city. And under the direction of Valmo Victor, you probably heard of him.
I haven't, I remember the name, but I can't place it. I'm trying to think of who I would ever know.

Yeah, but he's a great, he never did extend himself in the field, but he mastered music in his own way, playing an instrument, I mean really playing. And he's one of the, and we have quite a bit of the fellas who came along, you know, that started with us who really became top-notch musicians, that he started out in that profession. Who did he start out?
Who would you, do you remember any of the names?

Yeah, uh, yeah some of the guys is, uh, like, uh, on the west coast you have one of the trumpet players, Junior's Colton, he's playing with some of the better bands out on the coast. And, uh, we have a Tramon player, Danny, I forget his name, but he's a Tramon player, and now he's singing an emcee and all of the coast, I understand. And boys like, uh, we called him Lil' Jack. I can't think of Lil' Jack's last name at the time. He played with, I think he played with, uh, what, uh, not him, whatever.
What instrument does he play?
He plays trumpet. Jack Willis. Lil' Jack, yeah, I think it is, something like that. He played with one of the, several big bands. Jack Willis probably. Yeah. He's from here.

Wait a minute, I'm trying to think of another guy that's a guy. Wallace Davenport, he's played with several of the big bands from here. And then the other guy, I can't, uh, Joe, I know his name, Joe Newman.
Joe Newman, yeah, well Joe Newman, he's from here. He started music at the same time, you know, that I did. But he was in the Uptown section, I think his family was musicians.
Dwight was his father and he was a piano player.

Yeah, and he's one of the better trumpet players during that time, you know, that came along. I've never met anybody. He's still going strong, yeah. He knows a lot of people. I think he's playing with Lionel Halton I think. No, he's still with the cop.
With the cop, yeah.
He's been with the cop for years. He's done well.
I wanted to see him when I was in New York but they were playing at the Waldorf and I couldn't get in that place, you know. Yeah. That's a little out of my mind. Yeah.
Can you think of the names of any of the other blues your father played?
Would he play something like Baby Don't You Tell My Clothes or anything like that?

No, I can't think of any of the blues. I know some of the numbers, you know, I've forgotten them. They used to play a little bit, uh, uh, Ain't She Sweet, something like that, jazz number. Ain't She Sweet, see her walking down the street, you know, something like that. I can't recall that, you know, exactly. Oh yeah, I was just- But they used to jump that little, sort of a little jump number on it. And they played a lot of the old waltzes like, let me call you a sweetheart. I can remember some of those numbers, you know, that they used to play. That's it.
Did you have any other teachers? In music?
In music? I studied a while under Professor Humphrey, you know the Humphreys.
Which one is that?
Yeah, the old man. Jim?
Well no, because Willie plays clarinet.

Willie plays clarinet. Well they're father. I think his was Willie too. Yeah. The old man was named Willie. Well Willie plays clarinet and one brother plays trumpet. Percy. Percy, yeah. Well I studied a while under their father. He was a good musician too. He's taught me. He's still alive. Yeah.
Yeah.

He stays uptown. Oh yeah. I haven't seen him for years. And I studied a while under, I can't think of this. I got quite a few ideas from him too. He's one of the boys from downtown, not Levine, Levine was the head of the Grumwald School, Ape and Reed, man. He's from downtown. Where does he live? He played trumpet. He used to, Lejeune I think his name was. I think his name was Lejeune. He used to be a trumpet man. He used to play that dog. Oh, Dejeune. Maybe Harold Dejeune. Leo? Leo Dejeune? Could that be him? Harold Dejeune's brother?

That must be him. Yeah, one of the, one of the, we're talking man. Does he have a brother play sax now? Play zelto? Real bright font. Real bright font. Yeah. Has a red runnin mouthpiece on a zelto? Yeah, I think so.
Yeah, one of those. I don't know Leo.
You don't, yeah. But I know that's a big thing. I don't know. I don't know.
Yeah.
Yeah.
Well those, I got a few, you know, modern ideas from him using this high register without, you know, a great amount of pressure on the lip and et cetera.
Well when you started out on trumpet here in the city, what age were you?
Oh I was about 15 or 16. 15, making 16, about 15 years old.
Well who were the big men in the trumpet playing line?

In that time? One of the big men in those days in the trumpet line was the great Papa Celestein. He had a wonderful band at that time. And actually my idol, the great Louis Armstrong, was just about, you know, reaching his peak at that time. Did you listen to the record? You know, you remember Ken Rayner? I knew him. Yeah, well I used to listen to him. You know, I was very much inspired by him to be, on Sundays, this time of evening, you'd find them, they'd have a dance on Mondays, but they'd advertise it on Sundays and the bands would go around and they'd stop on the different corners and it'd really blow back. And sometimes two bands would meet up on these trucks, that's where this tailgate stuff came in, a lot of it. Tramon was sitting on the back of the truck where he could really get away with, you know, vamping slide. And Kid Rayner was one of the greats, you know, in that time. He used to, like Louis Armstrong said, he'd get down there and cut your head with that jazz, see. And he was one of the best head cutters for that stuff in my time. Because Loris and those boys had moved out, you know, and really had hit the big times. And Rayner was one of the greats that never did, you know, leave New Orleans and really go into the big, you know, big music award.
Do you remember Buddy Petit?
I can remember him not as well as, you know, some of the others.
Well, he died in 31, you know, so. Yeah. Right on there, so he'd be gone just about the time you were starting.
The time I was starting, yeah. So I started around 33, 32, around 31, around that time. Yeah.
Now, who else would you say was outstanding, either on record or here in person?

You mean back in the old, the jazz days? Back in those days. Yeah. Well, we had guys like, good Reed men like Handley. I mean, I used to listen to him a lot. I liked his, he was a real good, hard, steady rolling Reed man. And Henry Harden, he had quite an outfit one time. And now the day, you know, some of the folks who came along with me who still here around in the city, like the Knott brothers, the twins, they're Reed men. They're pretty nice musicians too. Back in place. I can't play, Sam.
What are their names?

One's named Duncan and the other one's named Edward. They're twins, they play, they're good Reed men. They play saxophone. They, uh, play with bands, you know, different outfits around town. Sometimes Larry. And Larry's had a good band, you know, he had his band around that time too. He started back in that time. I lived across the street from him and I used to listen to him. Then I'd rehearse him practically two or three times a week. And his brother John used to play trumpet and I used to listen to him quite a bit. And of course he switched to bass, you know, in the later years. Larry, he's always maintained the piano. He's had a good band through the years even until now.
Has Larry got a pretty good age on him by how old is he, you think?
Well, uh, Larry should be, he should be in his late forties.
So he really has come up in more recent times and say Rene Armstrong and those stuff.
Yeah, yeah, yeah, he was one of the, you know, came along just a little ahead of me because they were about six, seven years older than, you know, advanced than I was.
Now let's see, who else would you be listening to on trumpet? You must have heard some other people.

Um, that's about, you know, the guys who really, you know, I really was interested in listening to that playing. That's about all that I had though. You know, can remember offhand, you know, listening to. See?
What brass bands have you worked with?

Well I've worked with the Gibson brass band and that was the only jazz brass band, you know, that I played with outside of the school band when I was coming up with me. And I was, I got a chance to learn quite a bit, think about jazz more than ever. And because I ran into some of the old timers, you know, in that field, like Dave, and he'd give me a lot of ideas and things that I didn't know and he could hum it and I guess, you know, most of that stuff is played by Ed anyway and you catch the, you really get the knack of it. And I got experience of playing with, another trumpet player of one of the old times that I enjoyed having experience of playing was Kid Clayton too. Clayton, I played a film with him and boy he went back and got some of the old numbers like Panama Rag that I really hadn't heard of, you know, since I was small. And after a couple of courses I already came back to him and I found myself getting right in on it, you know, and it was quite an experience. And I got a chance to play my first film, you know, was with, I played along with Clayton. And that was quite an experience that I had longed for, you know, through the years. Because most of the time I never did go in for brass band music, you know, more or less.
Well he's mighty good, Clayton. Yeah, yeah.
He's a good trumpet player though. You know what I'm talking about.
Oh, you mean? Well, uh…
Do you know your stronger trumpet player than Clayton?

Well, I might be a little stronger but those guys had something to be treasured. I mean, you know, and you can only get it from them by playing along with them and observing it, getting in on it, because they don't write it on paper.
No. Well, he play all that stuff, man. Sure, I better tell them. The band I played years ago, so… These bands come in and you gotta catch with them.
Yeah.
I play through the band.
Yeah. A lot of other stuff, man.
Well, here they are. It's all new to the one but I got them covered. Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.

pages.label: 003_Dave Bailey and John McNeil Interview, 1959-10-25 Part 3

blocks.x: Well we're going to finish off with Mike Neal.
You done got me already.

No we only got part a year man. Part a year man. It's going to take two or three sessions for him. We want to play some records for him up at Tulane and stuff and get him to tell us about the bands on the records. But who did you play your first job with?

Well my first job is professional so you sort of speak is the way you get some money for it. We had a little outfit we broke off and organized on our own. And they was mostly I think we played for the Patterson's and we had one of the fellas who was a little more advanced. He's one of the greats around town. Now he's a tenor man. You might know. His name is John Patterson. I don't know him. I don't know him but he's real good. He's one of the better tenor men in town now today. He's been on the coast for quite some time. He's back now. And his daddy had a hotel down there, the Patterson Hotel. So he gave us the job playing on weekends down there for him. And that was how we started playing for the first little outfit. And so I played with John Patterson in a little outfit. You know of our own, see. And we thought we were going pretty good there for a while. And who else did you play with? Well I played with mostly bands that, none of the real big name bands. You know I mostly played with local outfits. And I played with Hal Kristoff quite a bit mostly. I know him. Yeah, well he's a good man too. And I can't handle it. I can't handle it. And that's about the size of it. Other than at times I get little outfits of my own and take a few little jobs when I had time. And even now I'm in the process of getting little outfits together to go back into playing regular.
Well now, who were some of the old time musicians that you had played with?

Well like I said, Clayton was one of the, on the trumpet I played with him. Like Dave here on drums I played with him. He's one of the best drummers in the field from the old timers. And well like I said, Hal Kristoff is relative, you know, he came, he's one of the old timers, so to speak. Not as old as Dave, but he's been around that field quite a few times.
I think I'm about the oldest drum player in the city. I don't believe in none of them playing drummers. And I don't care about none of all of that.
Well you work with Louis Kappa, now he's an old timers.

Yeah, I work with Kappa and. Who Kappa? Yeah. Who was that, the client player? He's a guitar and. Louis Kappa? And bass. Oh you mean that's all he played guitar? He plays the bass too. Yeah he played in the brass band with us.
Well that's Freddie Kappa's brother you know. Yeah that's Freddie Kappa's brother.
Yeah but he played in the band with us. In the brass band. Yeah. What's he called Freddie?
He died up in Chicago. Yeah that's right.
Freddie Kappa used to play the trumpets. Yeah that's a guy.
Oh well I know him.

So I know both of them. And he know my brother, the one who's playing with us now. Kappa. He know my brother. My brother Duck Onions. He called him Duck Onions. Bass player in the pool too. Boy I take that bass when we be playing you know. I got a track car belt right there tune in C. And we get there and he get on that bass, take that bass and turn it all around like that you know. I throw sticks up in there and catch me. When I was younger I used to jump in a chair and run all around and come back. Cheek don't try to do it to his team. And I used to play three sticks at one time. Three sticks. You know what I'd do? I'd have a drum stick between his legs. I'd have a stick under his leg by the same side of the drum stick. And I'd be playing it like my, he had my snare drum bass. I'd be playing and I'd be playing and I'd be playing and I'd throw that dry stick on there and reach down and hit that thing in that pan man.
You're juggling acting at the same time.

When I played in South Sea down in a few clubs I'd have my cymbal hanging up in the ceiling. Reach up in here. And then people would say I'd tell them I was drumming and go here can't I partner? Yeah it's good. Pretty good. I had a more holler last night. They said play Dave though. You didn't tell me that's a dream. I got on this solo. It was too bad boy. What number was this?
I composed that number.
You tell me your dream I tell you mine.
That's his crib level you know he solos on the bass drum. I solo on the bass drum.
Of course I can solo on but I make it better on that one. And I cut loose and they say go on here. I don't know if they're going to do that.

I don't think they're going to do that. Some of the other guys old times played along with us since I've been playing with you all. Who are? I know Freddie on the tram horn. He's one of the old times. Yeah. He rang the pretty got his horn.
Yeah.
What's his name? Freddie what? I don't know his last name. He's a pretty good tram man man. Yeah he played now. He played with Buster too. You know Buster the tram man. You know Buster Moore?
Yeah Buster Moore.
Yeah he's one. Yeah I'm trying to get him on my outfit now. You know he'll make a box.
Oh yeah.
And that's about the sound.
Yeah let's see now. I'm trying to think of who else is in that band. Eddie Richardson.
Yeah Eddie Richardson. Eddie Richardson. Yeah he's in that band.
Cal Blunt.

Yeah Cal's been around for quite some time too. Yeah Cal Blunt, Eddie Richardson, and Freddie Kepler. Freddie. Yeah well. Not Freddie David. What's his name? Louis. Louis Kepler. Louis Kepler. He's with us.
He played in the brass band though. And the snare drummer. How old is he?
George.
George. George Sterling. Yeah Sterling. He should be around about close to 60 years old. Around in the 60s or. I know he's over in the 50s. Yeah.
Yeah late 50s. George, if you look at it good George, look older than me man. That's true. Said the same must be in that letter, right? What you kept. That uh.
Yeah we looked at that one. He wanted to see it, I wanted to show it to him.

Well we can get it another day if you got a little hunt for it. Yeah. Maybe we better get back to Dave if you think that's the size of it. Unless you want to tell us some of your favorite trombone players or clarinet players and guys on the different instruments from the old days that you listened to.

Well I can tell you the one. Well I can tell you the one. He's not one of the real old timers but he's one of the, he's more or less, plays that type of music better than any of the later musicians, is Alvin Alcorn.
Yeah.
And he's a very good friend of mine and I admire him very much. And I like his playing. Well he's known the world over there. He has, yeah.
He's, yeah.

So he come along, you know after most of these old great guys who really played that stuff. What about Ricard? You know being the younger guys he played, he's more voiced on that type of music than any of the other fellas that I know of.
He never heard Ricard on trumpet I bet. No I don't think he heard Ricard.
You never heard Ricard on trumpet?
I don't think he's played trumpet no more.
I believe he's playing bass now. I've heard him play trumpet once but you know he broke his jaw, remember? Yeah.
I don't know how he done it. How he broke his jaw. He's all got broke. Tough guys.
Some tough guys beat him up you know. Beat him up, white fellas. Yeah. Oh yeah, some white fellas beat him up. He broke his jaw.
He was a good, nice trumpet player. Yeah. Must have been about five or six of them jumped on him.
Do you remember any trombone players from back in those times? No. I don't know. You remember any trombone players from back in those times?
You remember any trombone players from back in those times?
Yeah.
That kid the whole trombone player.

The only one I know that's still active is, that I know of is Bill Matthews. Oh yeah. He used to play the silver standard. I was listening to him when he practiced, wake out a little bit yesterday. I was around in his neighborhood. Where he live in? Mylon Street.

That's where Bill Matthews lived in. He used to live right down in the area. He moved up though. He bought his home and everything. Yeah, his nice place, that beautiful home. I haven't been up there yet.
You got a wife? Yeah, uh-huh.
Yeah. I collect next door from them.
You got children? No, I don't have any children. Just him and his wife.

Yeah. I think he looks well to him. He ought to have a good age on him too. Yeah, yeah, yeah. He ought to be more than 40 years old. Oh, he's way up. He's way up in his late 50s. Because you know the longer we lived in this world, the only way bound to give.
I tell him I don't care if I lived so long to look like a monkey. No difference. The role is honor. You can't stay young man.
No, that's right. You know, I'm a kid. You know, I'm a kid.

You know, I'm a kid. You know, I'm a kid. You know, I'm a kid. You know, I'm a kid. You know, I'm a kid. You know, I'm a kid. You know, I'm a kid. But dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear talk about them tired. Then people told me, ladies told me the other day, they said, my God, did you ever stop the other day? I said, sure. I said, I killed them for the time working me. They always complaining, the young fellas, I'm tired. Never hear me talk about them tired.
Yeah, we want to talk about the music field now.

Well, let's see, we got about 20 minutes of you and we got about 20 hours a day. How many guys? I'm trying to pick up some old musicians. Okay, well I'm going to ask you some questions. What happened to Camilla Todd? Is she still
around? The piano player, you ever know her? What her name? Her name, Camilla Todd.
I don't know her. Clarence Todd was her brother?
She used to play piano. Who she played with, you know?
Oh, I don't know. She's played with everybody through the years. I think she's played

with Celestine. Celestine? I remember the head of a woman who used to play with him. I remember with him. But I never did know her name, you know? She was a pretty nice piano player. Oh, he's had good piano players. Yeah. Probably it could be the same

person you're talking about. Well he always has women, except when he had Professor Moneta. Years ago he just about has always had women piano players as far as I can remember. Either that or no piano player. Of course in the old days they used to have no piano. No piano, yeah. Now let's see. Who did you play your first

job with, eh? Me? My brother's band. The first band I started with, my brother's band, young tuxedo. And then after that, then we got with Chris Kelly. We got with our band. Some of the boys went away in different things. Some of the boys died. Jewel Bond, the chamelecrant player, he died in Alexander. Jewel's Bond? Yeah, he died in Alexander.
Is he related to Millie and those guys or did he?

I don't know if he's related to Millie. Millie used to play with us too, man, the young tuxedo. Millie Bond, a chronic player. Sure. Millie used to like to play with me. I was playing with the old brother. What instrument did he play? The Siddly Days' meeting, trumpet. Bright brother, he looked like a white man. He was sitting at the band. Yeah. Then he met bands. So I don't know if he's playing anymore now. I know the last time he was at the hospital to come see somebody there, he had a cab line running. He was getting old. He was here.
A fella, Joe Phillips, plays trumpet. He was taking Sidney's band. They were pretty good. Yeah. Yeah, Sidney. Sidney, I think. Joe Phillips is a good trumpet man too. You don't know him.
Yeah, I know him from the street. He used to work a lot with Joey Williams.
Yeah, yeah. He's a good trumpet man too. I haven't seen him in a long time. Work with Joey Williams? I haven't seen him lately. Hmm? I haven't seen him lately either. I know.
Yeah, Sidney, stop playing music. He's running a cab line.
Well, Joe Phillips now, does he still have a band?

No. William Houston had taken the band in charge after that. First it was Desveen and he gave the band up and then Joe Phillips taking the band. Then the next thing I knew William Houston, well he had taken it. That's the original band up. Yeah. Of course they've had quite a few, you know, younger musicians in it to date. But some of the fellas who started out with Sidney and Desveen, they still play with Houston. Oh, yeah. Some of them went with Larry, some of the old times.

I wanted to stop playing music. He didn't want me to stop. I was going to resign. He said, what are you going to stop? All the girls told me I'm going to get into church. Stop playing music and go to John's church. You can't do both, huh? I don't know. My manager was doing it. He's going to belong to that church over there. The manager of the band is belonging to that church. Remember when he comes up to that night?

That's my argument with him. I'm trying to convince him that you don't have to stop playing music to go to the church. He seems to think you have to do one or the other to go to church or play the music.

So I'm about to win him over, I think, on that. All them girls always tell me. One time I'd say, yeah, there's a church right across the street in the house. I bet you ain't never been there yet. I'd go to church, playing that music. I'd say, that's all right. I'd say, God give me that gift. I had one that tell me, I let them call and say, God going to knock me down one day at the drum. He ain't knocked me down yet, and she's out there in the Hope Cemetery, and I'm still there. She was going to church. Christians. I'd let them down there and say, get drunk and everything else. They don't need to tell me what to do. God knows me. God knows when I'm wrong. He knows when I'm wrong. He knows when I'm wrong. He knows when I'm right. And I've got this much religion in there, I'm going to church. I can go to church nine times a day, but if this church ain't right, that church ain't going to do me no good. That's right. And you mean the church in your heart? That's right. That's the main church. That's all God wants is the heart. I don't know my heart's pure. I don't hold nobody in the heart. I'm going to be the whole lot of them to have them too, belong from the church. That's right. Well, back to your early days now. Who was in the band with your brother? Let me see. When we started that band, we had Willie Jones, that little brother, got killed by an automobile.

Willie Jones was one of the great, great Clannett brothers. I don't know if you knew him. I know his brother. I know John. John, yeah. John, I played with John. Well I played with John too. Yeah, but I'm talking about the one that John's playing. I'm trying to get him in this outfit that I'm getting together now on the bass. Well I take a few lessons from his brother Willie. Yeah, he's good. And he was a real good drunk man. Well voiced on music. Yeah, read music. Read real good.
Clannett, he played Clannett in sax. That's Kaiser.
That's the one that got killed by the car. They call him Kaiser.
Yeah, yeah. That's what they call him? Yeah, they used to call him Kaiser. Nickman.
He used to come home and teach me music when I was, you know, starting in the field.

He was good man. He was going to make up a band, take me here when he got killed. He had been in California since 1927. Come back here and was only here a month to see people that caught up on him on the static. Right there in the front.
In 47 he went to California. In 47. Yeah. About 27. Did I say 27? No, I said he went away in 1927. No, not 27 because he taught me music in the 30s.
Well then 27 he was with Louis DuBois. Yeah. Well, what was it? I can remember that.
He went to California during the war, right? In the fall.

Well anyhow, he was in California. Come back here to visit the people. They're only here a month. And this car hit him about 2 o'clock on a Saturday evening. Hit him at 4th Street and carried him all the way to the club. And didn't stop. Never stopped. Didn't catch that guy until about one or two weeks after that. Hit him. Hit him. Hit him. Hit him. Hit him. Run drive. And the fellow told me about it. I live on Chippewa Street upstairs. A fellow named Joe Williams. He said, oh David, come to the window quick. What up? He got me excited. What's the matter? He said, you know Willie Joe got killed? I said, no. No. He got killed for Saturday. Calls for a hit him. Hit him. Run drive. And the time he called me I was sick. I was back home.

Oh. But this fellow, I know you know him. He plays a guitar player. He worked at the quarters sometimes. He plays, he's still one of the banjo players. George, his name is George something. Kind of heavy built up brown skin fellow with a sort of large hair. And he plays the- Oh, Lawrence Marrero. No, his name is George. George Gano. I don't know his last name. Pre-old George. Pre-old George. Yeah. With those Bush-Countdowns, the government all the way across. Yeah. I played one of my first carnival jobs with him. We played two jobs on a carnival day. And the first experience I had to play on, during the carnival, on the trucks, like they have the Elks crew, you know. And that was quite an experience too. His favorite nom is, uh, Some of These Days. And we had quite a time. That's a good old nommer though. He plays, right? He's a good guitar, banjo. He's an old nommer, been a lot of new ones. I think he still sticks to the banjo too. Yeah. He's teaching guitar and banjo mostly now. Oh yeah. I saw him-

Well, he plays trumpet too? A few weeks ago, but I was close enough to speak to him. He's on the banjo. Yeah. He's still using banjo in some of them bands and them over there. It sounds good too. He tried to get rid of bass, violin, and the tramo, and bring it back. And Clonett too, he brought all that back.

My first experience of knowing that I was really hitting it, you know. I played with guys like him. That was my first experience of playing with somebody the whole time. Been playing with most of the guys.
What kind of music do you prefer most of all to play yourself? Myself?
Dixieland. Best music in the world, man. That rock and roll music song is rock.
Yeah. I like sort of sentimental music. You like sentimental? More or less, yeah. That's good too. Personal preference. That's good too. But I like the Dixieland style of jazz and so on.

Well you're relatively young to be playing with the bands that play Dixieland, it's surprising you know. There's not too many guys in their forties playing with them. No. Clemmer is working and he took Bill Matthews' place at the paddock. Oh he did? Yeah. And Bill Matthews is out of the paddock. He's been out a couple of weeks now. Oh yeah?
Clemmer Turbillons and that.
Yeah. And Frog can play good old style trombone. You know Frog?
Yeah, I heard that. Yeah.
He's working with Paul Barber on Monday night at the concert.
Yeah.
He and Lil Jack is on trumpet.

Lil Jack? Yeah, and Louis Cottrell is playing clarinet. What's Lil Jack? A little short talk. Yeah. Must be the same Lil Jack. He's all in the music. A little bit of a hook to his nose maybe. Probably the same Jack that started out with me. I think he's working with Ray Charles and Lloyd Brice. Yeah, yeah, he's been around. Yeah, he's been around. Old Ray Charles. Oh no.
Yeah, well he's making it now. He's really, he's got accepted, you know, Ray Charles. Yeah, this boy, this guy, I came along with Tom, Tom Jefferson, one of the trumpet players that played a lot.
Oh yeah. Tom and I used to go to school together too. We started.

I think I played a few jobs along with Tom, and he got him in a lot of it. And he plays a lot of Dixieland stuff. He had a guy play a trumpet with him, his last name is Joseph, I don't know his name, he's crippled. Well that's Frost.
That's Frost.

Yeah, well he's good too. Yeah. Yeah, well I remember I rehearsed with them when they had the band called the Crescent City High Hours, a bunch of youngsters around his age. I'd sit in with them several occasions on the rehearsals, you know.
Well Thomas Jefferson took over the band when Bill Matthews left, you see. Oh yeah. And he's in on trumpet now and he's got a trumpet with him.
Who do Bill Matthews play with now?
Nobody I don't think.
Yeah. Nobody? No. He just might as well just consider himself saying he'll stop playing.
Well he's only been stopped for two weeks.
For two weeks he's been in the paddock for quite some time. Over ten years now. Oh yeah.
Good Lord man, he's worn out, you know. Well Matt, he needs to stop for a week or two at least. Let me see. Now who was in that young tuxedo when you and your brother started? We got Willie Joseph.

Willie Joseph, his brother was one called Nelson Joseph. My brother on bass, I was on drum. And let me see who was playing trombone. I forgot who was playing trombone. We had a 7th grade officer, you know that.
Nelson Joseph played what?
Nelson Joseph played the banjo. That's how he was using banjos on it.
And who was the trumpet player?

I'm trying to think of him now. Who was. I'm trying to think of a trumpet player. I believe it was a brother called Walter Donovan. He's dead now. He was playing what, trumpet or trombone? Trumpet. He was playing trumpet. That band been rubble for so long.
Quite long. Because I was a brother on bass, I was drum.

Nelson Joe was on banjo. Willie Joe was on clarinet. And I believe it was a trumpet. And I believe it was Walter Donovan was on trumpet. I forget it's been so long, you know. And you can't remember the trombone player's name, huh? No. I can't think of what it was. Yeah. I can't remember what it was. Yeah. And you can't remember the trombone player's name, huh? No. I can't remember what it was. I think it was a fellow initiative.
Oh yeah.

Yeah, I can't think of his name. I can't call that man's name for nothing. Been so long, you know. But I know we had a good band. All I know that was good. We had seven pieces. And I can't think of his name. He was on Tramble.
Well, how long did that band stay out?
Oh man, it's been some time, man. How long was they together?
How long were they together?
Oh, we stayed together a long time. Good many years. Good while.
Were you playing together when they had the Big Storm or were you with Chris Kelly then?
They had the Big Storm in 1915.
Which band were you with then?

I was with my brother's band then. I had them. I was with Chris Kelly after that. But anyhow, I stayed with Chris Kelly after we stopped traveling, one, two, and all the different places. I played Chris Kelly six years. My brother, John, was in the band, so we played bass. We played together. Six years. And we went to Tallulah. And stayed up there for months. That was our headquarters. We played around different places.
Just a sec.

Lee Collins used to play with you? Sure. We used to play with my brother at the offensive band. Oh yeah. Sure. I said Lee Collins was getting killed down Lee County Hall. I'm sure of that. The Jewmaker was all killing by the ladies' friends. That sounds like the truth. I'm telling the truth. Look. You know what's happened? Another folks played at this place, you know? And he went down there and got to dancing with the Jewmaker. The ladies' friends. The Jewmaker's giving her a dance. That's a wild lady. Got to dance with her. And she got sweet on Lee Collins. Lee went to talk with her. She said, take care of man. That's my woman. Don't you put that woman in there. I'll keep care of your man. I said, come on. I said, come on upstairs. I can't leave by the head. I brought them upstairs. Remember that? The man was a killing. Were you playing upstairs in those days? Yeah. They called them. Yeah. The Hall of the New York State was upstairs. And they called them in the cooperators too. And New Hall, that was down on the third and the street. New Hall, played that.
That was upstairs.
I used to be up on Camp Street. Yeah. I went out and I got in my face. I said, come on. I said, come on up there.
You see that in the head, Lord? I said, I'm getting killed. No, it wasn't Lee Collins. I'll tell you that it was Walter Donaldson.

That fellow that I told you. He dropped there with us. He didn't drop there. He dropped dead from playing a parade up with the- No, but I'll tell you how it was. Was that Washington? When I was in the car, he was in the car. He was in the car. He was in the car. He was in the car. He was in the car. He was in the car. He was in the car. He was in the car.
He was in the car. He dropped dead from playing a parade up with the-

No, but I'll tell you how it was. Was that Washington? Was that Washington? Fourth and- Let me see, not Fourth. Sixth and St. Thomas. That's where the band was supposed to meet. It was in the summertime. Hot. We were all that on white shirts and black ties and things. And I don't forget what time it was we were supposed to leave there. He was rather late. And so when he came, so when he came, when he came there, he was late. And Brown, Chris Kelly was playing with Brown Band then. And this little fella called, let me see his drum player's name. I can't think of this little drum player's name. Sun White. Sun White, do you know Sun White? Yeah, his name is Edmund Washington.
I bet you didn't know that.

That's his real name. No, I didn't know it. Sun White. Well he live up on Long Street now, I believe. Back real quick. He was playing with them. I said, watch out, Blue. I said, Brown and Kelly's banger runs in today. You know what he said? He said, well, I'm going to toot this trumpet today. Brown and Kelly's nobody. I said, man, he cuddled us on the drum. We left him there and went down the fourth seat. It was hot that day, Fulton Thomas. We got a beer. It was all rain and wet. This from 6th Street to Fulton Thomas. That's how hot it was, rain and wet. So we went back, come back up and went back to Washington Street. And when I got to Magazine Street, he comes and starts playing the snare drum. And I don't forget who was playing the bass drum. And he kept on coming back on me and I told him to say, Walter Blue. That's Walter Blue you're talking.
Yeah, Walter Blue, yes. Yeah, I know who you're talking about.
Yeah. He says, and his son, he got a son, every time his son sees me, his son started crying. His son is working at Lutchen's now.
Yeah.

Every time his son sees me, his son, they're boiling, they drink, they see me, he started telling people about me and they started crying. About my dad. Every time I see him, it's a damn thing with my dad. And when we got most of the camp street, after we crossed Magazine, after Magazine is camp, he said, come on, let's play a number now. And the band started off, that man went way up above the steps, like Lou's what I said. And I said, I ain't never heard him blow like that before. And as soon as we got most of the grade, most of the college team, he got out to the parade. And look, he done this. And he ran to the gutter and he stuck his finger and everything like that. And I told my brother and I said, you all better stop us, that man's sick. Grandma and my brother said, oh come on, he's all right. I said, that man is sick. He said, let's stop. That man bad off. And when he vomited, he vomited. It was black paint, charcoal, and he vomited. And there's a no-called man later, a little iron picket pen. And he ran in there, tried to get assistance from there. Just that quick man. And he ran in there. And we had them went all the way to Pachanga. The police come back on horse, the police on horseback. Come back, and a colored woman with a little white bear like you know, a colored woman letting the white baby down. Run with the little drum. And I got there and fell flat on that pavement. He hid that pavement. And they picked him up, put him on the gyar. We had a mouth full of gold, diamond rings, pins, watch. Lately these nice looking fellas, you know. Bright fun. Had a hair like white boy, like y'all. Lately him up on the gyar and put a pill on his head. And we got there and he was just always saying, hmm. And they sent him to the hospital. Fifteen minutes after he got in the hospital in his day. That's right. And after that, after we played that parade, it got dark just like night. And when we got to the drive in Jackson, it was in the water up there. It was right in the thunder and lightning. Yeah. And I think about him a lot of times. And I know the tomb that he's buried in. And every time I pass on a Louisiana bus, I'm like I'm going to go to my barber first and I look at that tomb. He was a teamster, you know. And they put him in that tomb. And I look at that tomb. And every time his son see me, he'd cry.
Where is that tomb exactly? I like to see it.

It's a tomb just as you cross. Seventh Street. It's the second big tomb on this side. Right at the front. It's not the first one this way, but the one going to Washington. The first big tomb. I try to look at that. Shake my head. And I say, you know, I look at them gray. I say, I don't see how people can be so mean, white and colored, and always take one another life. You know, it's a sad thing, you know. To see how we got to leave here and never come back no more, you know. It is. It's sad.
I couldn't do that. I didn't do that. Is Blue's name on that tomb?

It might be. I don't know. I didn't. I'll ask his son. I'm so excited. But he's wasn't. I'll ask Young Blue. Hmm? It's been a long time. Because my first wife died in 1923. I was living on that. Where'd you get it? She was living when he died in 1923. And she was 29 years old when she died. And you know how old she would be now. In 1923. She's from Rhode Island, Louisiana. I shipped her by the way. I was a bearer. And that's when the time he died. But his real name is Walter Donison.
Robertson. Huh? Robertson.
Robertson?
Donison. His son told me his name was Blue Robertson. Blue Robertson? The little blue calls himself Blue Robertson. You know a…
He hung up with that one son of a day. He's a little son of a day.
He used to drink. He was brought up by I think Eddie Marrero or Simon or John. One of those brothers you know. Marrero, Moran they call him.
I don't know if he drinks. He used to drink. He drinks. He still drinks. I haven't seen him in quite a while.
Well this looks like a good place to stop. Let me turn it off. We should appreciate it. We're going to have to get together another day. I'll turn it off now.

segments.title: Interview opening and address
segments.summary: Allen opens the session with date and address and asks Bailey and Zander to identify themselves.

segments.title: Bailey's birth date found through marriage records
segments.summary: Bailey never knew his parents; he found his age (69, born January 28) through his marriage record at city hall.

segments.title: Birthplace, stepfather and half-brother Ernest
segments.summary: Born at Third and St. Thomas; his mother married twice, and his half-brother Ernest in Oklahoma last visited in 1927.

segments.title: Marriage in 1910, Spanish-American War and World War I
segments.summary: Bailey married at 21 in 1910, recalls no Spanish-American War, and says he was scheduled for the draft in World War I.

segments.title: First music Bailey remembers: shows, church and dancing
segments.summary: Bailey says he was too busy to notice music, performing in shows, church and as a dancer; he played Friday nights with a seven-piece band.

segments.title: Foster and Dude Lewis, Wesley Dimes and Eddie Morris
segments.summary: Talk about the deceased Lewis brothers, the trumpeter Wesley Dimes shot in Baton Rouge, and Eddie Morris in Bailey's band.

segments.title: Bands Bailey played with: Young Tuxedo, Kelly, Celestin
segments.summary: Bailey sums up playing with his brother in Young Tuxedo, Jack Carey, Chris Kelly for six years and Papa Celestin.

segments.title: First instruments and the harmonica
segments.summary: Drums were his first instrument; he also played harmonica, guitar, piano and others, and Allen proposes recording him.

segments.title: Harmonica and drum tricks
segments.summary: Bailey describes playing harmonica with a derby, imitating trains and playing a whole tune solo on trap drums.

segments.title: Teaching himself drums on tubs and pans
segments.summary: No teacher: he learned on tubs and boxes, nearly lost his delivery job, and his brother bought a pawn-shop drum set.

segments.title: Learning to read music with Chris Kelly and Port Arthur
segments.summary: Bailey took lessons in 1921 with Kelly, read music, played on the steamer Capitol, and went to Port Arthur with the Black Eagle band.

segments.title: Jimmy Jackson and the Gibson band; Doc Paulin
segments.summary: Explanation of how the band was named Gibson after Jimmy Jackson (Alphonse Spears), and the dispute with Ernest Paulin.

segments.title: Disliking crowds and outplaying a rival drummer in a church parade
segments.summary: Bailey says he never followed parades and hates crowds, then tells how he tied another band in knots with his drumming.

segments.title: Rival drummers and Bailey's confidence
segments.summary: More stories of drum contests and a rival's boasting, ending with Bailey's love of music and Sunday playing.

segments.title: Offers to leave New Orleans and his brother's playing
segments.summary: Bailey turned down offers from bands elsewhere and says nobody taught him; Allen asks about his brother's age.

segments.title: John McNeil arrives
segments.summary: McNeil joins the room and he and Bailey chat about a letter before the interview continues.

segments.title: McNeil's name and birth in Mississippi
segments.summary: McNeil gives his name and says he was born August 22, 1916, in Mississippi.

segments.title: How McNeil got into music
segments.summary: His musical family led him to take trumpet lessons.

segments.title: McNeil's father, a string-band musician
segments.summary: His father John Sr. played piano and strings, sang a blues about being black but sweet, and now lives in Chicago.

segments.title: Father as booking agent for New Orleans bands
segments.summary: His father booked string bands for dances near Baton Rouge, including violinist Dick Taylor.

segments.title: McNeil's school band at Lafon and its alumni
segments.summary: McNeil moved between New Orleans and Chicago, then joined the first Negro school band under Valmo Victor; alumni like Joe Newman are discussed.

segments.title: Tunes McNeil's father played
segments.summary: McNeil recalls waltzes and jump numbers such as Ain't She Sweet.

segments.title: McNeil's trumpet teachers Humphrey and Lejeune
segments.summary: He studied with Professor Humphrey and with a downtown trumpeter named Lejeune, who taught him high-register technique.

segments.title: Starting trumpet; Celestin, Armstrong and Kid Rena as idols
segments.summary: McNeil began about age 15, around 1931, listening to Papa Celestin, Armstrong and Kid Rena on truck-bed ad tours.

segments.title: Other local musicians McNeil listened to
segments.summary: Reed players, the Knott twins and Larry Hubbard's band are mentioned as local contemporaries.

segments.title: McNeil in the Gibson brass band and with Kid Clayton
segments.summary: McNeil learned jazz brass band playing from Bailey and Kid Clayton and defends the old-timers' unwritten knowledge.

segments.title: McNeil's first job and bands since
segments.summary: The Patterson Hotel job with John Patterson, local outfits, Hal Kristoff and the old-timers he has played with.

segments.title: Louis Cappa and Bailey's brother in the brass band
segments.summary: Discussion of the Cappa brothers and Bailey's brother Duck Onions on bass.

segments.title: Bailey's stick-juggling showmanship
segments.summary: Bailey describes juggling sticks, hanging a cymbal from the ceiling and soloing on bass drum.

segments.title: Old-timers in the brass band
segments.summary: McNeil and others name veterans such as Buster Moore, Eddie Richardson, Cal Blunt, Louis Cappa and George Sterling.

segments.title: Alvin Alcorn and Ricard's broken jaw
segments.summary: McNeil admires Alvin Alcorn; the others recall trumpeter Ricard, now on bass, who was beaten and had his jaw broken.

segments.title: Trombonist Bill Matthews and growing old
segments.summary: McNeil names Bill Matthews as an active trombonist; talk drifts to age and Bailey never complaining of being tired.

segments.title: Pianist Camilla Todd
segments.summary: Allen asks about pianist Camilla Todd and Celestin's women piano players.

segments.title: Young Tuxedo and Millie Bond, Sidney Desvigne's band
segments.summary: Bailey names his first band and members who died; talk turns to Sidney Desvigne, Joe Phillips and William Houston leading the band.

segments.title: Playing music and religion
segments.summary: Bailey and McNeil discuss whether one can play jazz and go to church; Bailey says God gave him the gift.

segments.title: Willie Jones (Kaiser), McNeil's teacher, killed by a car
segments.summary: Willie Jones taught McNeil and died in a hit-and-run during a visit from California.

segments.title: George Guesnon and McNeil's first carnival job
segments.summary: McNeil recalls banjoist George Guesnon and his first carnival truck job.

segments.title: Preferred music: Dixieland
segments.summary: Bailey loves Dixieland and dislikes rock and roll; McNeil likes sentimental music and Dixieland.

segments.title: Current trombone and trumpet jobs in Dixieland bands
segments.summary: Allen, McNeil and Bailey talk about who is playing where now: Matthews leaving the Paddock, Thomas Jefferson, Lil Jack and others.

segments.chapter: Young Tuxedo and Chris Kelly years
segments.title: Young Tuxedo personnel
segments.summary: Bailey recalls Young Tuxedo with Willie and Nelson Joseph, his brother and a trumpeter possibly Walter Donovan.

segments.chapter: Young Tuxedo and Chris Kelly years
segments.title: The 1915 storm and playing with Chris Kelly
segments.summary: Bailey was with his brother's band at the 1915 storm, then six years with Kelly, including Tallulah.

segments.chapter: Young Tuxedo and Chris Kelly years
segments.title: Lee Collins and a killing at a dance hall
segments.summary: Bailey recalls a fatal dance-hall incident, first thinking it was Lee Collins, then correcting to Walter Donaldson.

segments.chapter: Young Tuxedo and Chris Kelly years
segments.title: Trumpeter Walter Blue collapses and dies at a parade
segments.summary: Bailey tells how Blue, playing hard in a hot parade, fell ill and died within fifteen minutes; he recalls the tomb.

segments.chapter: Young Tuxedo and Chris Kelly years
segments.title: Blue's real surname and his son
segments.summary: Allen and Bailey sort out whether Blue's name was Donison or Robertson and talk about his son.

segments.chapter: Young Tuxedo and Chris Kelly years
segments.title: Closing the session
segments.summary: Allen ends the session and plans another meeting.
